content: Cholecalciferol, also known as Vitamin D3, is a specific form of Vitamin D. Structurally, it is similar to steroids such as testosterone, cholesterol, and cortisol, although it is classified as a secosteroid. Cholecalciferol exists in several forms. Calciol is the inactive, unhydroxylated form of Vitamin D3. Calcidiol, also referred to as 25-hydroxyvitamin D3, is the form found in the bloodstream that regulates calcium levels. Calcitriol, also known as 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3, is the biologically active form of Vitamin D3. The precursor to Vitamin D3 is 7-dehydrocholesterol, which is converted into Vitamin D3 only after exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation. This process produces calciol. Following UV exposure, calciol is transported to the liver, where it undergoes hydroxylation to form calcidiol. Calcidiol is then sent to the kidneys, where it undergoes a second hydroxylation to become calcitriol. Calcitriol is the active hormonal form of Vitamin D3, which is why Vitamin D is often referred to as a prohormone. Cholecalciferol is the form of Vitamin D commonly used in food fortification. Industrially, it is produced by irradiating 7-dehydrocholesterol extracted from lanolin, a substance found in sheep’s wool. For products where animal-derived ingredients are not desired, ergocalciferol (Vitamin D2), derived from the fungal sterol ergosterol, is used as an alternative. The absorption of cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3) and ergocalciferol (Vitamin D2) is approximately equivalent in healthy individuals. However, Vitamin D3 is three to ten times more potent than Vitamin D2 and has longer-lasting effects. Despite this, the human body has a lower tolerance for daily intake of Vitamin D3 compared to the upper limit for Vitamin D2, which limits the overall efficacy of Vitamin D3 supplementation. Current recommendations suggest equivalent doses of Vitamin D2 and D3, but some experts propose that the Recommended Daily Allowances (RDA) or International Units (IU) for Vitamin D2 should be adjusted to approximately ten times the daily intake of Vitamin D3 to account for these differences. Cholecalciferol is highly sensitive to UV radiation. Upon exposure, it rapidly but reversibly degrades into suprasterols. These suprasterols can further irreversibly convert into tachysterol.
